Trine is a puzzle platformer with some action thrown in there. You have three characters that you can switch between on the fly, similar to the old Lost Vikings game. You first have the most useful class, the Thief that can use a grappling hook to wooden ledges, a bow, and a flaming bow to light torches. Then you have the wizard that can magically make boxes by clicking or holding the right trigger and draw a box. You can also draw platforms and click and drag specific things to move them or get them out of your way. You can use your boxes and platforms to crush enemies. These first two classes are a lot of fun and have a lot of depth, but then we get to the third class / character, the warrior. He is just your straight up sword swinger, effective melee character.... with a shield that seems pretty useless.

The game is very beautiful, bright and vibrant. It is also very physics based and the physics feel nice. There are nice visuals with diverse settings and instead of cut scenes, the game just uses narrations as you play, which I greatly prefer. Since it is so visually beautiful, it can be a beast on lesser video cards, even at the lowest setting. Your platforms and boxes crush enemies, objects can be thrown into enemies or through destructible walls, the grappling hook lets you swing, and you can wrap hanging spike traps around platforms so they don't fall. I seemed to get the most fun out of unintentional things, such as teeter tauter platforms combine with Ferris wheel like platforms coupled with skeleton warriors jumping and sliding around to fill the room. The platforming dynamic of moving physics based platforming was a lot of fun.

The controls are very simple, and a controller is highly recommended. You have a jump button, a change weapon button, a trigger for drawing boxes or a grappling hook, two shift character buttons, the left stick controls the character, the right stick is like an aim for the bow, to draw platforms and to aim your shield (which is useless when you can easily dodge attacks). You can aim the bow and the longer you aim it, the further the arrow goes. If you don't like switching between characters, you can also play with a friend, but it is sad there is no online co-op.

Each character has their own health and mana bar, but the mana never really seems to run out with enemies constantly dropping potions. If one character dies, they're dead until you reach a checkpoint, even previous checkpoints. If all three characters die, then you simply restart at the last checkpoint. Its a forgiving system, which I'm happy about.

As you progress through the game, you'll level up to get your choice of skill upgrades. You'll also find new tricks and skills.

The enemies seem competent and dangerous enough. The basic enemy is the skeleton that comes in four flavors, standard, shielded, archer and pyro. They will jump over pits, climb, fall and do everything to get to you (except archers that stand and shoot). The enemy AI seems good enough so every situation can be different  There are also spiders and bats, but for the most part, that's it.

It is a quick game, about 4 - 6 hours, but still a fun play through (not as addictively fun as Guacamelee). There is some replay value here with collecting stuff from each level and no playthrough feels exactly the same due to the physics and AI. It was a good design choice to have collectables stay collected when you enter each level so you don't waste time getting what you already had.

If you can get it cheaper than $10, go for it. If you're not into puzzles, avoid it, because the combat is pretty shallow.

[h1]Quickly draw a box and smash everyone with it[/h1]

Trine is a nice puzzle platformer with beautiful graphics and fun gameplay.

You play as three characters. Hunter, warrior and wizard. You must complete levels by using your platforming skills and some brain.
Hunter has a bow and grappling hook. You can shoot enemies or jump over further distances with a grappling hook. You also can use fire arrows to light up torches in dark areas. Warrior has a sword and shield and is perfect for fighting monsters and passing through dangerous sections like shooting fire or falling objects. Wizard can create objects and place them into the world. You draw a box on the screen and box appear. You can place it somewhere so you could climb where you want, you can drop it on enemies to kill them or you create a little bridge.
You will need to switch characters depending on situation but i found mostly playing as a hunter and switching to other occasionally.

All levels are unique and each of them is really fun to play. It requires slightly different approach each time. There might chasm, fireballs shooting at you, a bunch of skeletons trying to kills, underwater areas, various objects you can move and so on. It doesn't get boring for a second.
Puzzles are pretty easy and many sections can be completed differently. There are some tricky sections when you need to be quick, precise and time your actions well. But the game isn't hard, it just requires you to adapt to the controls and learn each character.

Graphically it looks amazing, even for such an old game. Beautiful environments, great animations and physics. I was amazed by how good every level looks. It colorful, magical, let it be a forest, castle or a cave, everything looks like developers put a lot of effort into.
Ultrawide works fine out of the box so here's another positive.
Narrator voice makes it sound like a tale and makes you get immersed in this magical world. On top of that the soundtrack is quite nice too.

I'd say this is a must play game. It's cheap on sale so if you didn't play it yet i suggest getting it. I'm bad at platformers but this one doesn't seem too hard so for slower people like me it should be perfect and with right amount of challenge.
This is also pretty easy to 100% so achievement hunters should play it too.

I think we should have more of these games nowadays. Trine simply looks stunning! It successfully captures the atmosphere of a medieval fantasy world. 

To make it interesting we have 3 protagonists - a knight, a rogue and a wizard - but we can only use one at a time. And no, the wizard cannot conjure up lightning and summon creatures or throw fireballs at the approaching enemies. Amadeus can only create boxes, planks or triangles - objects with which you can proceed further ahead on each level.

And this is where Trine shines: There are many puzzles and you need to think and find the solution. Occasionally, you can progress fast but on your way you notice you have left some collectibles behind. So, while completing the game does not necessarily take long you are apt to spend hours with the game just to make a 100% progress on each stage.

Frozenbyte did a wonderful job when releasing this gem back in 2009. Instead of picking this one you should look for the complete edition which has its sequel, the DLC for the 2nd episode and the soundtrack included. Here in Hungary the retail version of the same bundle costs around 5 EUR and you can activate all the contents via Steam.

You cannot go wrong with this one and as Trine is regularly discounted you can easily find it for a suitable price. Just make sure to grab it with a friend as the sequel includes co-op mode!

“Long” version:
[u]Trine Enchanted Edition[/u] (just [u]Trine[/u] from now on, for the sake of simplicity) is a 2.5D puzzle platformer/adventure where you control 3 characters and make your way through countless classic fantasy locations. It was developed and published by Frozenbyte.

This one is going to be fun to write about!
You see, I played the original version of [u]Trine[/u] back in 2009. I was at uni and looking for something my terrible laptop could run. I was done with my second [u]American McGee’s Alice[/u] playthrough and wanted a side-scroller. That is how I came across [u]Trine[/u]. I finished it in a couple of days and really loved the atmosphere, how great it looked and how FUN it was.
In 2012, I got it on Steam, along with the sequel.

Anyways, let us begin.

You control 3 different characters – the Mage, the Thief and the Warrior.
After having their souls bound by an artifact called the Trine, the heroes must battle an undead invasion while adventuring through a plethora of classic fantasy locations, such as forests, graveyards, dungeons, etc.

Is the story anything to write home about? No, not really. But it is serviceable, charming and it keeps you entertained. I feel like that is perfect for a game like this. The characters are charming, they have distinct personalities and there are snippets of clever writing scattered throughout.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2743879786
Even though all three characters can do most things and solve most puzzles, they have clear strengths and weaknesses.
The Wizard has a harder time during combat, as he relies on summoning objects/telekinesis to solve puzzles and to keep enemies at bay. His offensive options are very limited. Movement-wise, he is also limited, however, this is mitigated by the countless objects he can summon, like platforms, boxes, etc.
The Thief can grapple onto wooden surfaces, so her traversal is unmatched. She can swing around the obstacles with ease too. She has access to a bow that lays waste to enemies – this weapon can be upgraded and becomes your main tool to dispose of undead hordes.
The Knight is the least interesting of the bunch, I am afraid. He shines during combat. However, the melee combat is not exactly deep – in fact, it is quite mashy. He does have some abilities that can aid during puzzles, but he is clearly outmatched by the other two characters. He does have a shield that blocks incoming projectiles, however; but as I said, what he can do, other characters can do too, sometimes even better.

Gameplay is divided into exploration/platforming and combat.
Exploration requires platforming, hence why I grouped them up together. It is also important to mention that puzzles and a good part of the platforming is physics-based.
As I stated, most of the traversal will be done with the Thief, as she can use her hook to nimbly move through the map, whereas the Mage is great to move objects around with telekinesis.

Combat is a bit mashy. If enemies are at ranged, you will spam arrows as the Thief; you will then switch to the Knight and mash the attack button until everything dies – there is little nuance to it. I do not think the combat system is inherently bad, but your regular attacks dispose of 95% of enemies and most of them have very telegraphed attacks that are easy to dodge.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2745795801
Graphics-wise, I feel like [u]Trine[/u] looks stunning. The colors are vibrant, the environments are detailed, vegetation is lush and particle effects are plentiful. Character models are a bit simple, but nothing too noticeable.

Sound is up next. There is something super charming about this game and how it sounds.
The narrator has a very soothing, trustworthy voice. The voice acting is a bit on the cheesy side, but I did appreciate it.
The soundtrack is very enjoyable and it sticks with you long after you played [u]Trine[/u].
Killing skeletons has a very satisfying “crunchy” sound to it and it is great!
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2743880486
When it comes to co-op, I know it should go under the gameplay section of the review but I wanted make a standalone paragraph about it.
This might be a hot take but… I think [u]Trine[/u] is a much better game when played solo. As I mentioned before, puzzles are physics-based and a lot of them required quick platforming based on weight. Having more players on screen can lead to a messier experience.
I played this game 3 different times on Steam with friends and I found myself going “Why am I not enjoying it? I don’t get it, I used to love this game”. After that, I gave it a rest and decided to enjoy it on my own months later. It worked. I loved it. I think it is just how a friend puts it – you can screw around too much, you can lock characters and never switch back (granted, you can allow 3 of the same character in the options). The game is also too zoomed in so you cannot move that far away from each other.

[u]Trine[/u] is a classic. I am glad I got it and I am looking forward to trying [u]Trine 2[/u]. I will opt to play it on my own from the start.

You can get it for cheap fairly often, during a sale.
Easy recommendation.

Final score: 8.5 out of 10.

[b][i]Trine Enchanted Edition[/i][/b] will appeal to retro gamers everywhere. The setting is delightfully old-fashioned. There is no post-apocalyptic wasteland or brown sci-fi dystopia. The game is set in a dreamlike fantasy world, full of enchanted forests and fairy-tale cliche. And it looks beautiful.

The basic gameplay is standard 2D platform but the meat of the action involves using the skills of your three characters to solve a variety of physics-based puzzles. The thief has a very handy grappling hook that allows you to leap over obstructions. The knight is, as you would imagine, the main offensive weapon. More interesting is the wizard who can create platforms and move things around telekinetically. And yes, flipping between the three  is key to solving the puzzles.

The combat becomes a bit of a chore later on, and distracts from the puzzling and sightseeing. Also the game is relatively short at around six-eight hours. Nevertheless, 2D platform games are practically extinct on all platforms but [b][i]Trine Enchanted Edition[/i][/b] is a gorgeous example of the genre.

[code]Trine makes for a great three player co-op experience, even for players with less videogame experience. A little more balanced & gameplay variety would’ve made Trine even better, however.[/code]

It’s pretty rare to see co-op games made with three players in mind. There are many videogames that can be played with three players, sure, but most co-op games are designed for two ([i]It Takes Two[/i], [i]Resident Evil 5[/i], etc.) or four players ([i]Left 4 Dead[/i], [i]Payday[/i], etc.). And while [i]Trine[/i] can also be played either alone or with just two players, it’s definitely at its best if it’s played by three players – and while online play is supported, I’d suggest resorting to couch coop, if possible. There’s just nothing better than sitting in front of a screen and arguing with your fellow players on how a riddle should be solved.

But let’s get back to the game itself. The original [i]Trine[/i] released back in 2009 and was so successful that it spawned a franchise currently consisting of four games. It should be noted that the original [i]Trine[/i] was replaced by its [i]Enchanted Edition[/i] in 2014 – a remake of the game using the [i]Trine 2[/i] engine as well as adding online multiplayer.

At its core, [i]Trine[/i] is a 2D platforming game with light puzzle and combat elements. There are three characters to play as, all with different abilities. The wizard is able to conjure boxes and planks, which help getting around obstacles. The knight is best at fighting, though he got a shield to protect others as well. Lastly, the thief can use a grappling hook as well as a bow to quickly move around and attack from afar. Combining the abilities of all three characters then, it’s mostly just about getting from the left side of a level to the right side, overcoming obstacles blocking your path.

Of course, as [i]Trine[/i] is a co-op game, these obstacles should require all three characters/players to work together, combining their abilities. I say “should” because in practice it will quickly become apparent that some abilities prove more useful than others. Most of the obstacles present in [i]Trine[/i] are platforming sections combined with environmental hazards (fire, gaps, etc.). You’ll quickly find out that the wizard (magical platforms) and thief (grappling hook) are most useful – sometimes even necessary – in climbing tall walls, repairing destroyed bridges, etc.

Meanwhile, the knight usually sees limited use. Sure, his shield is needed in some situations, like getting through a couple of spiked balls scattered across the floor. But his weapons? There are a few enemy encounters during each level, yes. These consist of either skeletons or spiders as enemies (a little more variety would’ve been great). And while the wizard might not have the best combat abilities, considering he can only smash magical boxes on their heads, the thief’s bow alone already makes for great ranged damage. As a result, the combat encounters are usually over so quickly that the knight swings his sword a few times – and that’s it. Most of the level is thus spent following paths the other two characters made. It would’ve been great if the knight’s abilities proved more practical.

Apart from this imbalance, [i]Trine[/i] provides fun platforming and light puzzles. Exploring each level is rewarding, as hidden treasure chests and XP potions offer items as well as upgraded or even entirely new abilities for the characters. It also makes for great fun to figure out where collectables are and how to reach them, during my playthrough, all of us three players were able to spot them where the others didn’t.

However, I feel like making the new/upgraded abilities entirely optional is a double-edged sword: One the one hand, you’ll never feel like you’re missing out if you haven’t found all collectables during a level playthrough. On the other hand, as new abilities are optional, all puzzles also remain solvable using just the basic abilities. As such, you’ll encounter the same challenges throughout the entire game. More variety, by making new abilities non-optional and actually design challenges just for them, would’ve been great.

Overall however, [i]Trine[/i] is very much a joy to play. Its simple controls work well and it’s easy to get into. The challenges on offer make for great co-op fun but aren’t too complicated as to really break the flow. Checkpoints are plenty and you’ll only be reset if all three players are dead at the same time. As such, even one player can usually carry others through the game, as long as the riddles allow it. Thus, [i]Trine[/i] makes for a great game even if players don’t share the same videogame experience.

If there’s a rule though, there also must be an exception. Thankfully it’s not the very few “boss fights” scattered throughout the game – they might even be a bit too easy (on normal difficulty at least). No, the big spike in the difficulty curve stems from the last level of [i]Trine[/i], [spoiler]Tower of Sarek[/spoiler]. Apart from only featuring two checkpoints (one at the beginning of the level and one near the end), it also requires significantly more platforming skill than the rest of the game. Combine that with constantly rising lava (= instant death) and you’ll get a challenge that’s quite a lot harder than the rest of the game.

I wouldn’t say the last level of [i]Trine[/i] requires outstanding platforming skills, in fact it shouldn’t pose a problem to anyone familiar with platforming games. However, if playing in a group with people who don’t like platforming sections at all, keep in mind that the last level might lead to some frustrations – especially as the constantly rising lava keeps the pressure up throughout the entire thing.

In terms of length, a playthrough on normal difficulty while collecting most of the collectables and without replaying levels took us three about 8h. The story of [i]Trine[/i], told between levels, is forgettable at best but it’s non-intrusive and the gameplay entertains more than enough for those 8h.

Finally, I want to praise the look and music of [i]Trine[/i]. It looks great and soundtrack also gives it wonderfully cozy & magic atmosphere. While the glow and bloom effect is a bit too intense for my taste, it can be [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/35700/discussions/0/537405286662155165]turned off[/url]. For a game that was released in 2014, it sure manages to hold up even in 2022. I also didn’t run into any technical difficulties and was able to use an Xbox One, PS5 and Switch Pro controller at the same time.

Concluding, apart from some minor problems, [i]Trine[/i] is a great game for lengthy three player co-op sessions. It makes for some light-hearted fun and (mostly) accommodates for players of different skill level. Just make sure you pick the character you want to play before everyone else (although those can be switched during levels as well).

The most chill platformer I have ever played and this is enough for me to already give this game a high score, because I am sick of platformers that are all about tight timings, precise movements and driving me nuts with unfair difficulties and game designs.

Seriously, I even enabled so called Hardcore Mode in Trine and still didn't rage even once. That is because Trine's difficulty doesn't depend dying and retrying same level/location/area over and over and over again but rather on clever and careful usage of abilities of 3 characters you can switch between and understanding physics of objects and enemies in this game. Once you get used to each character, completing levels and finding each collectable becomes just a chill playthrough at the evenings or weekends after work days.

Another strong point for Trine is how the game looks: the gamma, colors, saturation and details of environment do indeed give you the feeling of being sucked right in some tale about magical kingdoms, knights, wizards and so on. It was simply a pleasure for my eyes to look at every level of Trine.

Unfortunately there are some cons as well. Combat becomes repetative very fast because you either use bow (sometimes wizard's abilities) to attack from the distance or swith to knight and go close range with either a flame sword or freaking hammer which is, when upgraded, can strike lightnings (pray the Thor). Turning Hardcore Mode on turns enemies into fucking sponges and combat becomes just a left mouse button clicking simulator, unloading attacks on enemies untill they finally die, which is not fun. Speaking of enemies, there is basicly no variety of them present in Trine, you face basic skeletons, archer skeletons, skeletons with shields and at last beefed up skeletons aaaannndd thats it.... just skeletons... There are also 2 "bosses" which are essentially just higher hp enemies you defeat in the same way as skeletons, by spamming attacks at their weakpoints, nothing interesting.

Overall, I really liked the game and looking forward to buy and play all Trine games, this is the type of platfomers which I enjoy.

Trine: Enchanted Edition is a puzzle platformer where you play as a wizard, a knight, and a thief who are journeying across the kingdom, fighting the undead and searching for the artifacts that can separate the characters and save the kingdom. You can play by yourself or with up to two other people, cycling through the characters to fight enemies and solve a variety of puzzles.

The story in the game is pretty simple: 3 characters have to go on a quest to find a long lost object and save the kingdom. The story and characters don't have much depth, but that isn't necessarily an issue. The story doesn't really affect the gameplay very much, it just provides a backdrop to what's going on.

The puzzles and enemies in the game are fairly simple. There are a few areas where the puzzles are a little more tricky, but for the most part it was fairly simple. There are a variety of settings you can change, though, so some of the settings I played with could probably be changed to make things more difficult. In particular, having two players with unlimited characters and levitation meant that there were some jumping puzzles that were really easy to cheese with a couple of wizards levitating each other. 

Where the game really stands out is in the beauty of its environments. Every scene I played through was absolutely gorgeous, even considering the age of the game. The various forests and castles you go through all look really nice and the entire game has a really pleasant atmosphere.

Overall, Trine was a really nice puzzle platformer that was a lot of fun with to play with a friend. If you want a casual game with simple puzzles and beautiful atmosphere, this is a good choice. 9/10

A beautiful blend of action, platforming, and puzzling Trine manages to offer lots of fun and even some challenge. There are also some RPG elements through level ups, skills, and hidden equipment. I will admit, the story wasn't very gripping and my friends and I would often just skip it, but the gameplay is top notch.

Armed with a bow, the thief is the most agile of the three and you can use her grappling hook to traverse the environment. The knight is the traditional melee character and comes with a shield, sword, and a hammer. Probably the best character though, is the wizard. He can create boxes, planks and floating platforms, and he can also move them around. If that doesn't sound exciting, wait until your slinging boxes at all your enemies or throwing planks on your friends to make them fall into pits.

When you aren't busy knocking each other off of cliffs or into fire or spikes, you will find that Trine is an extremely well made co-op game. Everyone character and player really has to work together to get through the game, and everyone fills a role. The thief's grappling hook is perfect for those hard to reach places and she is often the one retrieving experience potions, though she can hardly do it alone and the wizards platforms help immensely. The wizard is arguably the leader of the team because he is able to carry everyone on platforms, disable traps by obstructing them, and he can handles enemies fairly well with his objects. Admittedly, the knight seems to have the short end of the deal as he really only shines in combat; he can throw boxes and break walls, but there are very few cases outside of combat where he is absolutely necessary.

Trine was the only local co-op game me and my friends would play for quite a while, it was just too good to put down. Now with the automatic update to Enchanted Edition, this game just got better. This game goes on sale often, and I buy it for friends whenever I can because this is a well made game and this is great developer. They worked tirelessly to completely update a 5 year old game that probably didn't rake in as much other less deserving games, and when they finished they just included it for every owner for free.

You might find find a better action platformer, or a better puzzle platformer, but you probably won't find a game that blends the two together well and offers a terrific co-op experience.
Beautiful game with some story telling and awesome jumping. Really liked those skill combinations of characters in jumping. And what most, you can play it in co-op mode!

A fun blend of fantasy and magic, [b]Trine[/b] evokes the timeless charm of a classic fairy tale. Even years after its release, the ability to switch between characters in its platformer setting, each with their own unique mechanics, remains engaging. I’ve spent the first few hours playing in single-player mode, and it’s been a joy. Next on my list? Trying it out in local co-op

A kingdom falls, and grave by grave, the dead arise. Taking advantage of the chaos, a thief slips into the Astral Academy to steal an artifact known as the Trine. On top of the Academy looking through his telescope is a wizard, and seeing the approaching army of the dead, heads down to hide the artifacts for safekeeping only to find a thief already inside. A Knight, in pursuit of the thief, charges into the academy hallways and without much thought, all three touch the Trine, their souls merging into one. To unbind their souls from each other, seek out three great artifacts, discover the reason the dead have risen, and save the kingdom from its peril.

[b]Trine[/b] is a light game that is easy to digest but offers gripping visuals, a mystical atmosphere, and enticing gameplay.  All of the features of the game are simple in design but intricate in execution.  The gameplay, aesthetics, and narrative all come together to create a whimsical and charming adventure. I highly recommend this for all gamers to consider; and for fans of the genre it is a sure bet.

By far the best aspects of the game are the stunning visuals and alluring atmospheric presentation of the setting. Each and every environment you explore is diverse, captivating, and charming. The ambiance really captures the mystical aura of the game perfectly. [b]Trine[/b] easily has one of the most immersive 2D gameworlds I have encountered in video games.

The gameplay is light and quick to grasp. Anyone should be able to dive right in, regardless of ability level. But various difficulty levels and a "hardcore" mode ensure that skilled players can still find a challenge. And whether you are playing on “easy” or “hardcore,” the gameplay is entertaining. Mixing elements of platforming, action, and puzzle solving with the unique identity of the game establishes an experience that is simultaneously familiar and novel— and irrefutably fun.

The story is whimsical and fantastic; and the characters are pleasant and endearing. This synergizes well with the aforementioned atmosphere to establish an amusing fantasy experience. But it also remains light and relaxed, and never takes itself too seriously.  So even casual fans of fantasy will enjoy the narrative.

[b]Trine[/b] is definitely a worthy pick-up. No matter what your standard preferences are, you should give this game some consideration. Check it out.

Trine is simply an excellent game, and even years after release it still stands as one of the standout platformers on Steam. It’s the kind of game that immediately grabs you with its charm and then keeps you hooked with smart, well crafted gameplay. The artistic design is a huge part of its appeal. The world is vibrant, colorful, and almost storybook-like, with beautiful environments that feel alive and magical. A lot of players still point to Trine as one of the best looking 2.5D platformers, thanks to its lighting, physics, and attention to detail. But it’s not just nice to look at the levels themselves are thoughtfully designed, making full use of the game’s mechanics. The core gameplay revolves around switching between three characters a wizard, a knight, and a thief each with unique abilities. This system is what really makes the game shine. Puzzles and platforming sections are built around using these abilities in creative ways, and while the mechanics are easy to understand, there’s a lot of depth in how you combine them. You’re constantly swapping between characters, and the balance is well done so that each one feels important rather than optional. Another area where the game gets a lot of praise is its accessibility. It’s easy to pick up, but still engaging, making it enjoyable whether you’re playing solo or in co op. Multiplayer, in particular, adds a fun layer of chaos and cooperation, as players work together (or accidentally get in each other’s way) to solve puzzles. It’s also worth highlighting the overall polish. For a relatively affordable game, the level of care is impressive. Controller support is excellent, the tutorial is clear and accommodates both keyboard and controller players, and the interface is clean and easy to navigate even in multiplayer. These small details go a long way and show the developers really put effort into making a complete, player-friendly experience. If there’s any downside, it’s that the combat can feel a bit simple compared to the puzzle solving, and the game isn’t especially long. But honestly, those are minor issues in what is otherwise a very well rounded experience.

[h2]When physics was still a novelty...[/h2]

Trine (2009) was originally released during a period where physics was still hot. You have to keep that in mind if you decide to play this great game in 2025 and onwards. That's still true for the Enchanted Edition, released in 2014, which is basically the original game using the engine from Trine 2.

If you're a regular gamer, I don't think Trine will pose too much of a challenge. It's more about the experience of sightseeing the amazing scenarios and having fun with the physics than mowing down the undead. That's so true that the creators didn't even bother to add different types of enemies.

With that in mind, be prepared to experience one of the best platformers out there. You play all the 3 characters as much as you like, since you can switch between them very fast. At a given point, it might make more sense to use the rogue to fire arrows and do some ninja-like acrobatics than using the knight, who doesn't have a great deal of mobility, but can fight like a maniac when there are lots of enemies on screen.

If the regular gameplay feels too easy (and it's likely that will be the case for most long-time gamers), try raising the challenge a bit by playing on Hard + hardcore mode and completing all the achievements. Laughing at the mistakes is a must, so don't get frustrated if things don't go well in multiplayer. ;)

Playing Trine is a very relaxing experience in general. It's a game focused on art rather than addictive gameplay. The soundtrack and beautiful sights will definitely pay off the lack of challenge.

Trine, developed and published by Frozenbyte, is a standout action-puzzle platformer that combines enchanting visuals with clever gameplay mechanics. Released in 2009, it offers players a captivating experience set in a richly detailed fantasy world where magic and mystery intertwine. The story revolves around three heroes—Amadeus the Wizard, Pontius the Knight, and Zoya the Thief—who are magically linked by an artifact called the Trine. This connection is the foundation of both the narrative and gameplay, as each character’s unique abilities are essential for progressing through the game’s intricate puzzles and platforming challenges.

The core gameplay revolves around switching between the three characters on the fly, each bringing a different skill set to overcome obstacles and solve puzzles. Amadeus can conjure and manipulate objects, creating platforms or levitating items to assist in traversal. Pontius is the muscle of the group, wielding a sword and shield to fight enemies and break through barriers. Zoya’s agility and her grappling hook allow for dynamic movement, enabling access to hard-to-reach areas. This trio-based mechanic encourages creative problem-solving and exploration, as many puzzles require combining their abilities in thoughtful ways. The physics engine adds a layer of unpredictability and freedom, allowing players to experiment with different solutions rather than following a strict path.

Visually, Trine is a feast for the eyes. The game’s hand-painted, storybook-like environments are richly detailed and filled with atmosphere. From lush forests and shimmering lakes to crumbling castles and shadowy caverns, every level feels like a piece of art brought to life. The lighting and particle effects enhance the magical ambiance, creating a world that invites players to explore its secrets. The fluid animation of characters and environmental elements further immerses players in this fantastical setting, contributing to a sense of wonder throughout the adventure.

The musical score, composed by Ari Pulkkinen, complements the game’s fantasy theme perfectly. The orchestral tracks shift seamlessly between serene melodies that underscore exploration and more intense, dramatic pieces during combat or high-stakes moments. This dynamic soundtrack plays a significant role in enhancing the emotional tone and pacing of the game, making each encounter and puzzle feel meaningful.

While Trine is highly praised for its innovative design and artistic presentation, it does present some challenges. The reliance on physics-based puzzles, while rewarding, can occasionally lead to moments of frustration when solutions are not immediately clear or when the physics behave unpredictably. Additionally, some players have encountered technical issues, such as performance drops or minor bugs, especially on less powerful systems. These issues, however, are relatively minor and do not overshadow the overall quality and charm of the experience.

In summary, Trine is an exceptional blend of puzzle-solving, platforming, and storytelling wrapped in a beautifully crafted fantasy world. Its character-switching mechanic adds depth and variety to gameplay, while the stunning visuals and evocative soundtrack create a memorable atmosphere. Despite a few technical hiccups, the game remains an engaging and imaginative adventure that appeals to both casual players and fans of the puzzle-platformer genre alike. Trine’s combination of creativity, challenge, and artistry makes it a timeless title worth revisiting.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
Trine is a puzzle 2D platformer game. You play as 3 different characters, (Wizard, Knight, and Archer) each with their own special ability usable to get through each level. These abilities are primarily physics-based, and most of the puzzles are solveable with a specific character in mind. The graphics are phenomenal for when it was released, and with multiplayer co-op available, this is a great puzzle game that achieves what it strives to be.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The storyline takes place in a ruined kingdom, which is incredibly instabile after the king dies without an heir. In events while the Astral Academy is being evacuated, the 3 main characters end up in the same spot and touch an artifact at the same time. This Trine object binds their souls together, and only lets one of them be physically present at a time. The plot is largely narrated, this is how you get most of the story plotline. This storyline kept me pretty engaged and interested, although it is easy to just skip through and play the game without the cutscenes and narration, as they don't add too much to the gameplay itself.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Trine uses typical WASD controls for movement, and mouse controls for the physics-based special moves. There is controller support, however I played with my keyboard and mouse. The Archer can shoot arrows and grapple, the Knight has his sword and his shield for a variety of moves, and the Wizard can move objects around with his magic. Your main enemies are the undead skeleton warriors and you will be moving lots of boxes to either stack and make a tower, or use with force to crush skeletons. The three available characters can be switched out by simply tapping 1, 2, or 3. The backdrop graphics look amazing for a game released over 10 years ago, and is definitely one of the higher points in this title for myself.

The background audio in Trine is very ambient, which I'm a fan of as it is almost impossible to get tired of listening to. The three main characters have voice actors and the majority of the plot is delivered by a narrarator, but I have no complaints about either as they are both performed well. Nothing too special for the audio in this game, everything seems pretty standard for a game of this age. This game took me about 10 hours to complete.

[h1]Pros[/h1]

[b]Fun Puzzles[/b]
This may seem obvious, but many times I play puzzle games that aren't fun all the way through. The puzzles presented in Trine are not so difficult that you get upset when you can't figure them out, but starts you off easy in level 1, then gradually ramps up the level and puzzle difficulty.

[b]Character Selection[/b]
The ability to switch between the 3 characters on the fly is done very well, and helps keep the game fresh and new.

[b]Amazing Level Backdrops[/b]
As stated previously, the backdrops to each level are incredible, and were part of the main reason I initially gave Trine a try. Playing this game with the audio and visuals cranked adds a lot of atmosphere to this puzzle platformer.

[h1]Cons[/h1]

[b]Repetitiveness[/b]
The only gripe I have with this title is that it gets a bit repetitive overall towards the end. The level design and objects used do get a bit old towards the last few levels, however the place the game ends is perfect, and this is only a slight con. The fact that there are diffent puzzle types and strategies for each of the 3 characters helps the game stay fresh, and if there were only one character available it would make slaying the skeletons a whole bunch more boring.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Trine was one of the first games I started and (eventually) completed on Steam, and I think this is a great title for someone who is just getting into gaming, or a puzzle fan looking to add a classic to their collection. The Trine series is currently on their 4th release, which tells you a lot about the franchise if they are able to make 3 more games after this one, all with relatively glowing reviews. The ability to switch between characters with the press of a button, and the amazing graphics this game displays are definitely the strong points of this game, and if you're looking for a unique, older, puzzle game and Trine is on sale, I suggest you give it a try!

While 2D action adventure games have all but disappeared from retail, the genre is very much alive on digital distribution platforms like PlayStation Network, Xbox Live Arcade, and PC. Trine is the latest of these neo-classic games and it's an impressive, modernized take on the sort of effort that dominated through the 16-bit era. It does feel a little unfinished, as though the developers ran out of money or were pressured to get the game out the door. Still, Trine is a lot of fun and definitely worth playing. 

Gamers have control of three unique characters: a thief, a wizard, and a knight. Each has their own abilities they can use to traverse the game's environments and dispatch of enemies. The thief wields a bow and arrow and can grapple to wooden surfaces. The wizard can move objects with his mind and summon blocks or bridges. And the knight is the fighter of the group, best used for hacking through the undead army plaguing the world. The thief and knight give players the choice to use ranged or melee combat, and both can be equally effective. A typical example of the sort of puzzles the trio will encounter would be a seemingly impassable chasm -- the thief could use her grappling hook to swing across or the wizard could summon a plank and stroll to the other side. 

Most predicaments can be solved in multiple ways and you could make it though most of the game with just the thief or the wizard (the knight is really only useful in combat). There are instances, though, where you'll have to use multiple characters in tandem to proceed. The wizard might be able to get a hanging block swinging from side to side. The thief can then grapple to it, and the block's momentum will allow her to jump to a previously unreachable area. 

Our heroes' goal is to free themselves from the curse that has bound them together and rid the land of the usual evil that has consumed it. Along the way they'll solve puzzles, kill lots of skeletons, and earn experience points that can be spent to gain new skills. A lot of the green vials that contain precious experience points are hidden, so there are many secrets to be found for players that want to put in the effort. 

If you're playing Trine by yourself the three characters inhabit one body and you can switch between them on the fly. They each have independent health and magic meters, and if one perishes you'll have to get by with whoever's left until you reach the next checkpoint. The game can also be played by three people cooperatively, with each controlling one of our heroes, but this completely changes the experience. When playing by yourself, you only have to worry about getting one body past an obstacle. In multiplayer, each person needs to figure out how to get their character from point A to point B, making the game more difficult and stretching every little challenge out. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but other inconveniences get in the way of making multiplayer an optimal experience. The camera will let players wander off screen, for instance, where they can be killed by who knows what and that person will have to sit around until the other players find the next checkpoint. 

Trine is a physics-based puzzle platformer, meaning the game's objects and characters are governed by the laws of gravity and react realistically to each other and their environment. There are lots of subtle details and nuances to be seen here. Arrows can slip through cracks in wooden planks. The thief can aim her bow in 360 degrees, as can the knight with his shield. This allows for precision aiming with the thief, and requires you to direct your blocks with the knight. 

Man oh man, this is one good-looking game. Set in a medieval fantasy world, developer Frozenbyte has crafted dense, extravagant scenes that scroll by as you work through the adventure. Although players can only move on a 2D plane, the world is rendered in 3D and the camera will zoom in and out for cinematic effect. The renaissance music is also very well done, with catchy tunes arranged in a lush orchestral score. A narrator and the heroes are brought to life by talented voice actors. 

My favorite thing about Trine is that there is something new to discover around every corner. From beautiful vistas to interesting new game mechanics, the developers always seem to have another trick up their sleeve. There are just a couple aspects that seem phoned in. It could have used a greater variety of enemies, for one. Save for a few bats and spiders, you'll spend the entire game fighting skeletons. Spawn points warp skeleton after skeleton into the world, which always feels like a rather cheap and obnoxious mechanic. There are just two boss types that are reused multiple times: a giant skeleton, and some sort of beast with a turtle shell that is a pushover. Finally, your fight with the end boss will be quite anticlimactic, and there isn't much reason to return after you've completed the story.



The Verdict:

Trine is great fun in single-player and it's worth experimenting with the three-player co-op even if the game works best as a solo experience. Players are given a set of tools (three characters with unique abilities) and are presented with problems that can be solved in several ways, resulting in an adventure that feels wide open despite being relegated to a mere two dimensions. The beautiful visuals and sound bring this world to life and there is something new to discover around every corner. A lack of enemy variety, disappointing conclusion, and the wonky multiplayer keep Trine from greatness, but this is still a highly recommended puzzle platformer.

This is like an improved version of Lost Vikings on the SNES. The levels look enchanted. A lot of fun to play. The game runs smooth. Interface is good. Sound/music is good. Can be played by casual gamers like me. Perhaps a bit easy for die-hard platformers, but the looks make up for that. I can't find anything bad about this game. Absolutely recommended.

English:
I only heard good things about the game and now I played it myself.
Trine is a wonderfully designed game that has enchanted me with its art design.
Its three heroes are skilfully implemented in the game. Each character has his or her special skills, which must be skilfully used in combination to make it through the 15 - increasingly more challenging as the game progresses - levels to succeed.
The levels are entertaining and fun. Collecting all chests and exp bottles is a small challenge. What I like is that the collected bottles and opened chests are stored. When you play it again only those that are missing will be displayed.

The replay value for the second time play through in heavy mode is given. But then it is over.

This game is joyable for everyone. It's combine action and puzzle altogether. The result is great.
Graphic is beautiful for me, like the details of environments and musics is just suit perfectly.

If you're looking for some fantasy game, pick this up. :)

Trine is a side-scrolling puzzle platform game with beautiful scenery, a fantastic soundtrack, challenging yet fun level design, and an interesting story to boot. Whether you play this game solo or with friends/family you will not be disappointed. I played it years ago but had to pick it up again because of how much I love it <3

Some games, we call them timeless because they don't really show their age. Well... This is not one of them lol. You really know it's an old game the moment you see the game resolution thingy where all old game does. It also plays like an old game too. 

HOWEVER, it was fun. It was pretty short. We got every achievement pretty easily too. You should play it whether you are doing a Trine Marathon like us or it's on your library and you want to play something.

Gotta get sick more often I tell ya.. anyways, Trine is modern day embodiment of old Vikings where you control 3 characters, each with their own skillset, and combat bad guys and puzzles in a story of restoring the balance (or save the world, who knows).

🔼 A beautiful 2.5D fantasy tale with an atmospheric dark fairy world and a divine soundtrack. A trio of unusual heroes united by a spell and now they're trying to save the world from the undead invasion. A half-educated wizard, a well-fed knight and a clever thief have a wide range of skills to solve entertaining puzzles. The battles are simple, the gameplay is great. Find secrets, equip items. do you remember the old Vikings game on super nintendo? well this is basically what Trine is, three guys with well defined abilities which have to be used in order to finish the levels. There is not much action per say but some of those puzzle will require patience and timing. Now there are times where the physics is not perfect and can make finishing a level a bit tideous. Also, if you are not into puzzles, I would not really buy it. I love puzzles and had a great time with the game. The graphics are amazing and controls overall is good. Lots of things to find even though it is just a side scrolling game. I would recommend the game. There is also a coop options which is interesting.

A year and a half ago I made a review about this game specially for Adult Elite Gamers group as I got the game from Humble Trove. Now I've had it quite a while in Steam as well and finally got enough time to finish this with all the Steam achievements.

The game talks about 3 persons who are drawn to the same place, because the world is in peril.
They get stuck on a 3-sided crystal which takes them to an adventure together. You can play with all 3 of them and change them on will. Even though this game is quite old it's still really enjoyable. They give you enough skills to level up. You can get gear to boost your stats. You can run, charge, shoot arrows, jump, shoot yourself over the screen like spider-man. The physics were quite fun and on top of that it has a little taste of a puzzleish game as well. Having to think where to go and how to get to certain points. You can draw different shapes and use magic to move them around. you can break walls, ceilings and walls either with the material the game gives, arrows or a big holymoly hammer or just throw the items with your warrior. The graphics are really gorgeous and enjoyable, not to mention the music. The last isn't quite something you could go around and hum all day, but it's still beautiful and fits with the game perfectly. Honestly where was this game when I was little. I would've played the hell out of this :D. But I enjoyed playing this even now when I am older. Basically this game is fun no matter the age.

Thoroughly disappointed after seeing the reviews. I expected a charming character driven experience but instead found minimal characterisation, story and dialogue, repetitive boss fights (there are seriously only two repeated throughout the game) and bland enemies (of which there are four), easily solvable physics "puzzles" and a deeply disappointing ending and final level. The environment design looks nice even if some assets are repeated but that is not enough to make this game enjoyable, replayable or even recommendable.

Here goes my review of Trine after 100% game completion with all steam achievements.

Enjoyment:
While the game is not a long one, it is deffinitely enjoyable one. I started the game on hard difficulty and I feel that it was a good decision. It was easy to die if not careful and completing every level felt rewarding (especially once you find all secrets in every level). I like that you can approach each puzzle or obstacle in multiple ways and there is never only single solution. As you progress through the game, you get much more tools to solve the puzzles which helps to keep the gameplay fresh and not repetitive.

Gameplay:
Movement and character animations are very good. The physics in this game works really well and the flow of the game is pretty nice. There were not any places where I got stuck so it felt like very smooth and enjoyable ride.
The monsters variety is very poor with only skeletons and few mini bosses and combat is very simple one too so in this aspect, there is definitely room for improvement.
Each of the three heroes has its own abilities and uses and you have to use most of them in each level to complete the puzzles. But even after finishing the game, I felt that Knight was the most useless one of the three and there were many levels where I have not even used him.

Story:
Mostly narrated between each level with few heroes dialogues at the begining of each level. Other than that, there is not any lore or information about the world of Trine outside of those I mentioned above. The story itself is very simple one and not really worth remembering. But I certainly didn't play the game for its story so it's fine.

Graphics:
I played Enchanted edition and I was pretty surprised how good the game looks. Beautiful colour pallete, great lightning and very carefully crafted level design. The graphics are certainly the strong point in this game despite its age.

Audio:
The game has pretty good and fiting soundtrack which adds to its enchanting atmosphere. Voice acting is rather good too, especially narator.

Technicals:
The game runs smoothly without any FPS drops. In 10 hours I spent in the game, there wasn't a single freeze and only one crash due to alt-tabbing (alt-tabbing was kinda broken for me).

I adore Trine!
I love it's lighthearted, whimsical fantasy world.
The side scrolling 2D world is so lovingly crafted!
And, if you happen to own an nVidia 3D Vision setup, then Trine is possibly the most incredible 3D game you will ever play on your PC. Slightly ironic as it essentially a 2D side scroller, but this game has incredible 3D depth in it's enviroments which, as mentioned before, are utterly beautiful and so well crafted!
Nice game to relax, there are some puzzles and little bit fight but still, a wholesome game to chill.
